The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers In OpenAI’s telling, the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”. Advertisement Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent, according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive. OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri. As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide. What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash. In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to. How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “ AI as Normal Technology ” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident. The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “ impossible ” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms. Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies. In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.” Further AI reading After much fanfare, Anthropic has listed on the stock market at $83 a share, giving it a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. It is the second big AI firm to go public this year, following SpaceXAI in June. The Economist has a great piece on whether the AI industry can ever make enough money to survive. It calculates that it must produce $3 trillion in revenue by 2030 to cover the costs of planned data centres. That is roughly equivalent to a tenth of all wages in high-income countries, or similar to the amount spent on food. Are people really going to buy as much AI as they do food? The Cambridge Dictionary has named “ human ” as word of the year, as a pushback against the growth of AI. It feels a bit like trying too hard to be relevant, in my view. As the COP31 climate summit continues, only nine countries have signed a pledge aimed at limiting the environmental impact of AI. As I have written previously, we cannot afford to run this 21st-century technology on a 20th-century energy supply.
summary: California has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI concerning an incident in which Hugging Face was attacked by activity originating from OpenAI’s servers. The suit alleges OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, and OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit.
author: New Scientist

title: Study finds U.S. data centers cause 650 premature deaths via distant air pollution
content:
A new study by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology quantifies how the rapid expansion of artificial‑intelligence data centers harms air quality and public health far beyond the sites of the facilities themselves. By linking hourly electricity demand from data centers to emissions from generators across the United States, the team estimates that the additional power use in 2023 produced roughly 650 premature deaths nationwide—about 5.3 percent of all electricity‑related mortality in the country.

The researchers built a modeling framework that tracks how data‑center electricity demand propagates through the nation’s interconnected grid and how resulting emissions travel under varying atmospheric conditions. The model incorporates emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) from more than 10,000 generators, then feeds these data into a chemical‑transport model that simulates formation of fine particulate matter (PM₂.5) and ground‑level ozone (smog). Translating the added pollution into health outcomes using epidemiological evidence yields an estimate of 513 premature deaths from PM₂.5 and 137 from smog.

Although the bulk of data‑center electricity consumption was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas, the highest per‑capita mortality rates appeared in Midwestern states such as Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota and Kansas. The mismatch arises because generators that respond to demand spikes in Virginia often lie in the Ohio Valley, where older coal‑ and natural‑gas plants emit more pollutants. Atmospheric transport further carries these emissions into downwind regions, where conditions—such as agricultural ammonia—enhance PM₂.5 formation.

The study’s senior author, Professor Noelle Selin of MIT’s Institute for Data, Systems, and Society and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, emphasizes that health impacts extend beyond communities neighboring data centers. Rural populations, in particular, face higher mortality risk because of the spatial distribution of power plants and prevailing weather patterns. The authors suggest that siting and operational decisions for data centers should incorporate air‑quality considerations alongside traditional factors like land and energy costs.

Future work will explore the air‑quality effects of onsite power generation at data centers and assess how flexible operation schedules might mitigate emissions. The research, co‑authored with MIT graduate student Yuang (Albert) Chen and collaborators at the University of California, Irvine, and Yale University, appears in the journal Environmental Research Letters and was funded in part by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.
summary: MIT researchers estimate that extra air pollution from data‑center electricity use in 2023 led to about 650 premature deaths in the United States. The highest per‑capita mortality rates occurred in Midwestern states despite most data‑center power demand being in Virginia and Texas, showing how grid emissions and atmospheric conditions spread health impacts.
author: MIT News

title: MIT engineers create dry, stretchy material to replace ultrasound gel
content:
Engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Singapore‑MIT Alliance for Research and Technology’s Wearable Imaging for Transforming Elderly Care (SMART WITEC) project have created a dry, stretchy polymer that can replace the conventional ultrasound coupling gel. The new material is designed to transmit ultrasound waves efficiently while remaining stable without the need for liquid replenishment, a limitation that has hindered long‑term wearable ultrasound devices.

Current practice requires a cold, water‑based gel to fill microscopic gaps between a probe and a patient’s skin, ensuring clear images. The MIT team’s earlier wearable patches used a hydrogel layer, but the gel dried out within a day or two, reducing acoustic performance. By engineering a solid polymer with a “bottlebrush” molecular architecture—backbone chains bearing dense side‑chain bristles—the researchers reduced friction between polymer chains, allowing the material to behave acoustically like a gel while staying dry from the start.

Laboratory tests on synthetic “phantom” models showed that the material transmitted ultrasound waves clearly for about nine days of continuous operation. In a treadmill experiment, a volunteer wearing a patch of the new polymer on the chest experienced no sweat buildup, whereas a conventional silicone rubber patch became water‑logged. A field demonstration involved affixing a key‑fob‑sized patch with an integrated probe to a volunteer’s neck; the device recorded uninterrupted blood‑flow images during a 30‑minute bike ride across the Cambridge‑Charlestown area.

The study, reported in Science, lists postdoctoral researchers Shu Wang and Runze Li as co‑lead authors, with additional contributions from MIT faculty Xuanhe Zhao, Chen Gong, Won Jun Song, and collaborators Zihan Tang and Ying Li (University of Wisconsin‑Madison), Chwee Teck Lim (National University of Singapore), and Xiaodong Chen (Nanyang Technological University). Zhao, Chen and Lim serve as co‑lead principal investigators of the SMART WITEC group. The work was supported in part by the Singapore‑MIT Alliance for Research and Technology and the MIT Health and Life Sciences Collaborative.
summary: MIT and Singapore-MIT Alliance researchers developed a dry, rubbery material that can replace the wet gel used in ultrasound imaging. The material enabled a wearable ultrasound patch to produce clear images continuously for nine days, even during vigorous exercise.
author: MIT News

title: MIT and Dana‑Farber researchers find code sharing rare in clinical prediction studies
content: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated? Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work. “Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.” While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code. This is where an international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute sought to help, by examining how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies. Such studies develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes, such as the risk of developing a disease. Because these models inform decisions about patient care, researchers need to be able to scrutinize how they were built and tested. Using large language models (LLMs), the researchers examined nearly 4,000 papers to identify statements about shared code. They then followed the statements to assess hundreds of associated code repositories. Their review revealed two key gaps: Code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings, recently published in Nature Medicine, are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Following the code TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. To understand current code-sharing practices, the team identified studies citing either guideline. The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models, and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central’s open-access collection. “The challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent. First, we had to identify whether or not a paper shared code” says Thomas Sounack, the study’s first author. He adds that authors “discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways.” The team used an LLM to help screen papers, identify statements about code availability, and extract links. Software then retrieved the linked repositories — online collections of code and related files — for further assessment. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed. It also assessed repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. “The real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text. These models helped us work with information that was scattered across papers and software repositories, rather than neatly organized in a table,” says Pollard, who is a senior author of the study. “That allowed us to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies.” Human reviewers evaluated the work of the LLMs. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results. Agreement was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Because classification errors remain possible, the authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact. Inconsistent code sharing Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Where code was shared, the contents of repositories varied widely. Some repositories were “extremely well-organized and -documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all,” Sounack says. Good code sharing, he explains, means “giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper.” Practices also varied substantially across journals and countries. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice. Some researchers, for example, provided synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where the original patient records could not be shared publicly. Setting a standard for code sharing Researchers who share code are already making an effort to make their work transparent. But clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ. TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. “We want to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code, and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors,” Pollard says. “The review gives us evidence to inform those discussions."
summary: Researchers at MIT and Dana‑Farber used large language models to review nearly 4,000 clinical prediction studies, finding that only about one in eight shared code and that many repositories lacked sufficient documentation. Their findings are informing the development of TRIPOD‑Code, a reporting guideline to clarify what code should be shared.
author: MIT News

title: Field Museum scientists identify new 300‑million‑year‑old amphibian ancestor
content: Scientists at Chicago’s Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor that lived more than 300 million years ago in a swampy landscape that covered the region. The find offers new clues about the early evolution of frogs and salamanders.
summary: Scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor that lived more than 300 million years ago. The discovery offers new clues about frog and salamander evolution and indicates the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape at that time.
author: Science Daily

title: Sodium particles cause hydrogen flames to shift from orange to nearly invisible
content: Hydrogen flames can change from a bright orange hue to being almost invisible when trace amounts of sodium are present in the surrounding air. Scientists note that this finding may improve safety in future hydrogen‑powered stoves and ovens by allowing visual flame detection to be replaced with dedicated sensors.
summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible due to tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say the discovery could make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find tiny bacterium under skin of deep‑sea sea pigs
content: Scientists have identified a previously unknown bacterium living beneath the skin of deep‑sea organisms called sea pigs, indicating an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe possesses an unusually small genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA encodes surface proteins, some of which are exceptionally large. Researchers suggest the bacterium relies heavily on its sea‑pig host for survival, while the benefit to the host remains unclear. The discovery highlights a novel host‑microbe relationship in the deep‑sea environment.
summary: Researchers discovered a bacterium living beneath the skin of deep‑sea creatures known as sea pigs. The microbe has an unusually small genome with over a quarter of its DNA dedicated to large surface proteins and appears to depend heavily on its host, while its benefit to the sea pig remains unknown.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists study why Ozempic and Wegovy cause varied weight‑loss results
content: Ozempic and Wegovy have been shown to produce dramatic weight loss for some individuals while yielding disappointing results for others. Scientists are investigating whether a hidden energy‑saving response in the body might explain these differing outcomes and could help develop more effective, personalized weight‑loss treatments.
summary: Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others. Scientists are investigating whether a hidden energy‑saving response in the body could explain the difference and enable more effective, personalized weight‑loss treatments.
author: Science Daily

title: Gut bacteria produce sulfur gases that cause terrible‑smelling farts
content: The unpleasant odor of flatulence comes from tiny amounts of sulfur‑containing gases that gut bacteria generate while digesting food. Scientists explain that certain foods boost these gases, that a loud fart is not always the smelliest, and that human noses have evolved to detect such potent odors.
summary: The secret behind truly terrible‑smelling farts is tiny amounts of sulfur‑containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists explain why certain foods increase the odor, why loud farts are not always the stinkiest, and how human noses evolved to detect these strong smells.
author: Science Daily

title: Brain study finds similar neural activity for free and forced decisions
content: New research shows that the brain uses surprisingly similar neural processes for both free choices and forced decisions, with activity building toward a decision before action occurs. The finding challenges assumptions about free will while indicating that personal preferences and experiences continue to shape what people choose.
summary: New research shows the brain uses surprisingly similar neural processes for free choices and forced decisions, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The finding challenges assumptions about free will and suggests personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.
author: Science Daily

title: Extinct Peruvian pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had extremely crooked face
content: A 6‑million‑year‑old whale discovered in Peru has been identified as the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo. Researchers noted that its skull is dramatically distorted, with an enormous downward‑curving snout, giving it a face that appears extremely crooked. The unusual asymmetry led scientists initially to suspect post‑mortem damage, but further analysis suggests the shape was a genuine evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor. The team proposes that this whale may represent the most asymmetrical facial structure recorded in any mammal.
summary: The extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo, which lived about 6 million years ago, was discovered in Peru. Its skull shows an enormous downward‑curving snout and extreme facial asymmetry that researchers interpret as an adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find fungal toxins in all 212 UK plant‑based foods tested
content: A new study examined 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the United Kingdom, covering categories such as meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk and soy milk. Researchers found that each product contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin, known as a mycotoxin. The study notes that mycotoxins are natural compounds that can contaminate grains, legumes and seeds during farming and storage.
summary: Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk and soy milk, and found each contained at least one fungal toxin. The toxins, known as mycotoxins, are naturally occurring compounds that can contaminate grains, legumes and seeds during farming and storage.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil, see them as key moon food source
content:
A new scientific report claims that potatoes could become a crucial food source for future lunar missions. The study documents that the tuber was successfully cultivated in simulated lunar soil, demonstrating that it can grow under conditions similar to those on the Moon.

According to the report, sustaining human life during prolonged lunar exploration will rely on life‑support systems that can produce food locally. Potatoes, with their high yield and nutritional value, are identified as an ideal candidate for such systems.

The research was conducted by scientists on a project backed by NASA, which concluded that the successful growth of potatoes in lunar‑soil simulant supports the feasibility of in‑situ food production for a future Moon base.
summary: Scientists reported that potatoes were successfully cultivated in simulated lunar soil. The Nasa‑backed project concluded the humble potato could be a key food source for a future moon base.
author: Guardian Science

title: Voyager 1 reaches one light‑day distance from Earth
content: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a. M. PST (5:16 a. M. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday. “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.” Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers). Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data. Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances. “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.” In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it. “Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.” Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, transformed our understanding of the solar system through their exploration of the outer planets. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made spacecraft to enter interstellar space. On Nov. 18, 2026, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Milestones, challenges Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018. “The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.” Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer. As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world. “We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.” For more information about NASA’s Voyager mission, visit: https://science. Nasa. Gov/mission/voyager/ -end- Abbey Interrante / Karen Fox Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1600 abbey. A. Interrante@nasa. Gov / karen. C. Fox@nasa. Gov Calla Cofield Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, Calif. 626-808-2469 calla. E. Cofield@jpl. Nasa. Gov Share Details Last Updated Nov 19, 2026 Editor Jessica Taveau Location NASA Headquarters Related Terms Voyager 1 Heliophysics Heliophysics Division Jet Propulsion Laboratory Science Mission Directorate The Solar System The Sun
summary: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026.

title: NASA hot‑fire tests RS‑25 engine No. 10001 at Stennis, supporting Artemis missions
content:
NASA performed a hot‑fire test of RS‑25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at the Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Nov. 18, 2026. The developmental engine was fired for the planned 200 seconds—three minutes and twenty seconds—by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions.

Although this particular RS‑25 will not fly, the test is intended to capture critical data that can be used to improve engine performance and reliability for future Artemis missions. For each Artemis launch, four RS‑25 engines generate up to two million pounds of combined thrust to propel the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket.

The upcoming Artemis IV mission, slated for 2028, will launch astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. That mission is described as a key step toward exploring the lunar South Pole, establishing an enduring human presence on the Moon, and building a foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

All RS‑25 engines undergo testing and are proven flight‑worthy at NASA’s Stennis facility before being used on SLS flights. The November test adds to the data set supporting the agency’s broader lunar exploration goals.
summary: 1 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA conducts a hot fire test of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St.

title: Astronaut photographs Lake Pelku from the International Space Station
content:
An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed Lake Pelku, visible near the center of the image, while the station passed over Asia. The photograph was taken by Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and is credited to CSA/Joshua Kutryk.

The International Space Station is described as a unique platform for Earth observation, employing both hands‑on and automated equipment. Station crew members have generated hundreds of thousands of images that record real‑time phenomena and aid research and disaster‑relief efforts.
summary: An astronaut on the International Space Station captured a photograph of Lake Pelku near the center of the image while the station orbited above Asia. The ISS serves as a platform for Earth observation, with crew members producing hundreds of thousands of images that record real‑time phenomena and support research and disaster relief.

title: New cryptography-based method finds pulsar PSR J1622−7204 1 million times faster
content:
An international research team has unveiled a new computational method that can locate pulsars in NASA’s publicly available Fermi Gamma‑ray Space Telescope data up to a million times faster than previous techniques. The breakthrough, described in a paper published Thursday in Physical Review Letters, was achieved by applying a cryptography‑inspired lattice algorithm to 15 years of gamma‑ray observations from the Fermi telescope.

Using the new approach, the scientists identified PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar that spins 261 times per second. The detection required only the equivalent of ten hours of processing on a standard computer processor, whereas the best earlier method would have needed a processor to run for roughly 600 years to achieve the same result. The algorithm, developed by Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay of the Weizmann Institute of Science, reformulates the pulsar search as a problem of finding the shortest vector in a high‑dimensional lattice—a technique originally created for breaking encryption systems.

Lead author Daniel Pook‑Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute), explained that traditional searches must explore a four‑dimensional parameter space—spin rate, spin‑down rate, sky position, and another variable—requiring an impractically large number of calculations. By converting the search into a geometry problem, each trial of the new algorithm runs in about five minutes on a single laptop core, making the process feasible on ordinary hardware.

The team plans to extend the method to locate pulsars in binary systems, where a companion star’s gravity distorts the pulsar signal and has previously rendered such searches ineffective. Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute and co‑author of the study, noted that tens or even hundreds of similar pulsars may already be hidden in the existing data set. He added that the next phase will combine the lattice algorithm with the crowdsourced computing power of the Einstein@Home volunteer network.

The discovery underscores the impact of NASA’s open‑data policy. Since its launch in 2008, the Fermi telescope has scanned the entire sky every three hours, and after an initial calibration period all data have been released publicly and continue to be updated. Open software tools such as NASA’s Fermitools enabled the researchers to prepare the dataset for analysis, and the accessibility of the archive allows any team to replicate or build upon the work, a point emphasized by Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
summary: 5 min read NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, illustrated here, scans the entire sky every three hours as it orbits Earth. Its publicly available data helps scientists find the rapidly spinning cores of dead stars, known as pulsars.

title: NASA TTT launches public challenge on life in 2075 with $20,000 prizes
content:
NASA’s Transformational Tools and Technologies (TTT) is soliciting public input on conceptual ideas regarding life in 2075. The challenge invites submissions exploring how future aviation or aerospace systems could improve efficiency, manage resources, reduce costs, and strengthen trust and transparency. Additionally, ideas should address how these systems can connect communities, improve access to services, and support future national priorities. Participants are asked to provide conceptual rather than technical proposals.

The initiative offers $20,000 in total prizes for selected submissions. Registration for the challenge opens on November 13, 2026, with a submission deadline of January 18, 2027. Individuals interested in participating can find registration details, rules, and eligibility requirements on the CrowdPlat website.
summary: NASA’s Transformational Tools and Technologies (TTT) is gathering public perspectives on life in 2075 and invites conceptual ideas about future aviation or aerospace systems. The challenge offers $20,000 in total prizes, with registration opening on November 13, 2026 and submissions due by January 18, 2027.
author: NASA News

title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
content: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github. Com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook. Com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu. Be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=40904862, August 2024: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=41390449, May 2025: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is. This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt. We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built. The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook. Com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams. We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code! The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day! Comments URL: https://news. Ycombinator. Com/item? Id=50562320 Points: 78 # Comments: 66

title: Sila signs $1B-plus deal with Panasonic to supply silicon‑carbon anodes
content: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US. Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time. This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics. Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry. We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021. Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain. The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO. Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying. This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech, have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year. The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics. China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it. Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.) I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority. “I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.” This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.
summary: After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US. Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Australian team keeps human liver alive 7 weeks; Sila signs $1B battery deal with Panasonic
content:
The weekday newsletter The Download delivers a snapshot of recent developments in technology, covering three headline stories: a record‑setting experiment with a human liver, a billion‑dollar battery supply agreement, and a new index that measures AI hype.

In Australia, researchers have kept a donated human liver alive outside the body for seven weeks, surpassing the previous record of roughly two weeks. The team connected the organ to a system of automated pumps and sensors that supplied nutrients, delivered blood, and removed waste. The experiment, reported by Antonio Regalado, suggests that the approach could open new avenues in biomedical engineering, including repairing damaged organs, growing new ones, and even exploring artificial wombs.

A separate story highlights a significant shift in the U.S. battery market. Sila has signed a contract with Panasonic Energy to supply silicon‑carbon anode material that could be worth more than $1 billion. The deal is intended to help Sila scale production and potentially bring smaller, lighter batteries to market. Casey Crownhart notes that the factory backing this partnership received a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department, underscoring a growing focus on geopolitics within the battery industry.

The newsletter also introduces the AI Hype Index, a tool designed to separate reality from hype in the AI sector. The latest edition tracks AI’s influence across diverse areas—from literary prizes and cyberattacks to a Grok‑ified version of The Odyssey. The index offers a quick snapshot of what is shaping the industry each month, and the newsletter lists several high‑profile AI stories, such as Anthropic’s record‑breaking IPO and China’s pursuit of AI‑powered weapons, as part of its “must‑reads” section.
summary: Researchers in Australia kept a donated human liver alive on a perfusion system for seven weeks, breaking the previous record of about two weeks. Sila announced a deal with Panasonic Energy to supply silicon‑carbon anode material worth more than $1 billion, backed by a $1.4 billion Defense Department loan.

content:
Sony’s WH‑1000XM5 headphones are now available at their lowest price ever, with all four color options in stock. Best Buy lists the model for $169.99, a steep cut from its $399.99 MSRP. Recent listings have shown the headphones for $198 at Amazon and $199.99 at Costco, indicating a broader price drop across retailers.

The WH‑1000XM5, launched in 2022, remain a strong offering despite the newer WH‑1000XM6. Reviewers note the XM5’s active noise‑cancellation as competitive with current Bose and Apple models, and its sound profile as tighter and more balanced than earlier Sony headphones. Minor drawbacks such as a bulky case and an all‑plastic construction are noted, though the reduced price makes them less significant.

The successor, the WH‑1000XM6, is also on discount for Black Friday, priced at $348 at Amazon and Best Buy, down from its $450 MSRP. A mid‑range option, the WH‑1000XM4C, sits between the XM5 and XM6 in price and features a foldable design. Reviewer John Higgins remarks that the XM4C’s noise‑cancellation falls short of the XM5, recommending the XM5 at its current sale price. Shoppers can take advantage of these ultra‑low prices both in‑store and online before Black Friday.

title: FCC votes unanimously to let prisons jam cellphone signals
content:
The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously on Thursday to permit state and local prisons to jam cellphones. The FCC stated that the new rule aims to address an influx of contraband cellphones used to commit crimes from within prison facilities. Although jamming devices are generally prohibited under Section 333 of the Communications Act of 1934, they are currently utilized in some federal facilities.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr asserted that providing correctional facilities with this technology will prevent prisoners from engaging in illegal activity. He noted that inmates use these devices to order hits, run drug operations, and traffic women.
summary: The Federal Communications Commission voted unanimously on Thursday to allow state and local prisons to jam cellphone signals. FCC Chair Brendan Carr said the rule will help prevent inmates from using phones for illegal activity.

title: Google adds collapsible AI chat sidebar to desktop homepage
content:
Google is adding an AI‑focused feature to its desktop homepage worldwide. In a post on X, Google’s vice president of product Robby Stein shared a GIF that demonstrates a new collapsible sidebar for AI chats.

The sidebar can be opened by clicking a gray bar on the left side of the screen. Once expanded, it displays a list of searches made in “AI Mode” and provides options to start a new thread, search existing threads, or connect a Gemini Notebook.

Stein’s post indicates that the feature is being rolled out globally, allowing users to easily find and return to their AI conversations directly from the Google homepage.
summary: Google is updating its homepage to include AI searches. In a post on X, Google's vice president of product, Robby Stein, shows how you can now open a collapsible sidebar to view and continue your AI chats.

title: Apple hires engineers to develop its own AI agent
content:
Apple is seeking an engineer to lead the development of a proprietary AI agent, according to a job listing identified by Bloomberg. The proposed assistant is designed to execute various tasks, such as web browsing, operating across multiple applications, writing code, and contacting services. This initiative would allow Apple to compete with similar offerings from other technology companies, including Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks.

Several of these competitors already possess capabilities to control computers via Mac applications, with Google recently expanding its Gemini model to perform similar functions. The job posting highlights Apple’s effort to build an agentic AI assistant that can manage a broad range of user-directed activities.
summary: Apple is seeking an engineer to lead creation of an agentic AI assistant that can browse the web, work across apps, write code, and call services, according to a Bloomberg‑spotted job listing. The project would put Apple in competition with AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet and Google’s Tasks.

title: Male mice that watch fights learn to defend better, study finds
content:
Scientists have used a mouse model to investigate why humans are drawn to violent entertainment. A recent paper published in Nature reports that male mice that observed other mice fighting performed better when later challenged by stronger opponents than mice that had no such exposure.

In the experiment, researchers divided male mice into three groups: fighters, spectators, and novices. Over eight days, each group received three 10‑minute training sessions per day. Novice mice played with stuffed mice in isolation, while spectator mice watched pairs of fighter mice battle from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier. This arrangement allowed the spectators to see, smell, and hear the fights.

On the ninth day, all mice faced a “fight night” against a formidable opponent in three 4‑minute rounds. Each bout was filmed from above to allow detailed behavioral analysis.

To track brain activity, the team genetically engineered the mice’s excitatory neurons to glow green when activated and inhibitory neurons to glow red. They also implanted optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions, enabling simultaneous monitoring of activity across the brain during the fights.
summary: Researchers assigned male mice to fighter, spectator or novice groups and gave them eight days of training with three 10‑minute sessions per day. On the test day, spectator mice that had watched other mice fight performed better against a stronger opponent than novice mice, according to a Nature paper.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google to roll out global Android developer verification in January 2027
content:
Google has announced that it will extend its Android developer verification program worldwide in January 2027. The program, introduced last year, already blocks the installation of unregistered apps in several countries this fall and will soon apply to all regions. Developers who have not yet registered are urged to do so before the rollout.

Under the new rule, apps downloaded from the Play Store will continue to come from verified developers, and the requirement will now also cover apps from third‑party sources. When verification is active in a user’s region, sideloading apps will be prohibited unless the developer has registered with Google. Verification requires the submission of government identification and a $25 fee, a measure the company frames as a security improvement.

In September, Google launched verification in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore, and Thailand without major incidents. The company previously indicated a 2027 global rollout and now confirms that the requirement will reach all devices within “several months” of the January start.
summary: Google announced Android developer verification last year, and despite numerous objections from developers and users, the company is forging ahead. It began blocking the installation of unregistered apps in some countries this fall, and the system is expanding globally soon.
author: Ars Technica

title: UCL and UNESCO study finds LLMs can give incorrect climate answers when prompted
content:
Many researchers have long examined how people encounter climate science information, focusing on the top results that Google surfaced when it still served links, as well as on social media posts and coverage in newspapers and television. With large language models (LLMs) now forming a significant part of the public information diet, it has become important to understand how these models handle climate‑change content.

A study led by researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) sought to address this gap. Because LLM output is delivered ephemerally to individual users and confined to a chat session, there is no direct way for researchers to track the information people have actually seen. The study therefore tested LLMs with a variety of prompts and evaluated their responses.

The researchers began with benchmarks of simple factual questions—questions that might already be present in the models’ training data—and then moved on to more complex interactions, including scenarios where users challenge the model’s answers. The study evaluated 33 different models, covering multiple versions of major frontier and open‑weight models. The flagship frontier models examined were Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.6 Flash, and GPT‑5.6 Sol. A full list of the models used is provided in the report.
summary: Researchers from University College London and the United Nations Educational, Scientific, and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) evaluated 33 large language models on climate‑change queries. Using both simple factual benchmarks and more complex prompts where users push back, the study found the models can provide incorrect climate information.
author: Ars Technica

title: Google to launch data‑center satellites on Blue Origin's New Glenn in 2029
content:
Blue Origin announced on Thursday that its New Glenn launch vehicle will carry Google’s data‑center satellites to orbit in 2029. The payload is part of Google’s Project Suncatcher, a research initiative that the company described a year ago as a “moonshot” aimed at creating scalable orbiting data centers.

The mission will place satellites, each offering computing capacity comparable to a data‑center rack, into a Sun‑synchronous orbit where they can draw nearly continuous solar power. Travis Beals, senior director of Project Suncatcher at Google, said the dedicated Blue Origin launch marks a “crucial milestone” as the company seeks to expand AI infrastructure in space by leveraging abundant orbital solar energy.
summary: Blue Origin announced that its New Glenn rocket will launch Google’s Project Suncatcher data‑center satellites to Sun‑synchronous orbit in 2029. Each satellite will have computing capacity roughly equivalent to a data‑center rack and will draw nearly continuous solar power, according to Google senior director Travis Beals.
author: Ars Technica

title: Black teens sue Baltimore County schools, police after AI gun alert misreads Doritos bag
content: In October 2025, four Black high school students were sharing Cool Ranch Doritos after football practice, winding down and waiting for their rides home. It was then, in the lull of a moment any teen with after-school activities knows well, that the school’s AI gun detection system suddenly flagged one teen holding a bag of chips as a potential gunman. Within two minutes, Baltimore County Public Schools officials who reviewed security camera footage linked to the alert determined there was no actual threat. They recognized the Doritos bag and canceled the alert, which notified not only other school officials but also the Baltimore County Police Department that no response was needed. The false alert could have ended there—before a traumatizing campus clash with police—but it didn’t. Read full article Comments
summary: Black teens sue Baltimore County schools, police after AI gun alert misreads Doritos bag.
author: Ars Technica

title: Russian national Igor D’iu indicted for spying on Silicon Valley firm aiding Ukraine
content:
Federal prosecutors have indicted a 25‑year‑old Russian national, Igor D’iu, on suspicion that he acted as a Russian spy targeting a Silicon Valley technology firm that provides assistance to Ukraine. According to the indictment, D’iu photographed employees and their computer screens while they worked in a coffee shop near the company’s Palo Alto office and compiled a list of home addresses for staff members and a senior executive.

The filing also describes an incident in which D’iu followed a female employee, identified in the affidavit as “FEMP1,” as she traveled from Palo Alto to San Francisco. Prosecutors say D’iu pursued her for nearly thirty miles, making evasive turns, running a red light and entering a grocery‑store parking lot before the employee called 911. She was directed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department’s Mission Station, where she flagged a patrol car and reported the chase; D’iu left after police made contact.
summary: Russian national Igor D’iu indicted for spying on Silicon Valley firm aiding Ukraine.
author: Ars Technica

title: Report finds MAHA PAC spent more on steak and luxury club than on candidates
content:
A Stat report examining the finances of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) political action committee shows that the organization’s spending patterns during the recent midterm election cycle favored non‑candidate expenses. The report, which analyzed the PAC’s financial documents, found that the MAHA PAC, headed by Tony Lyons, allocated more money to allies, boosters, meals, luxury items and its affiliated nonprofit than it did to political candidates.

The spending data contrast with a spring announcement by Lyons that he was leading a $100 million fundraiser intended to increase MAHA’s influence in the midterms. According to the report, the PAC actually raised $3.2 million and spent over $10.5 million in the election cycle, with more than $7 million of that coming from previously collected funds. The findings raise questions about the group’s priorities amid the movement’s broader midterm losses.
summary: Report finds MAHA PAC spent more on steak and luxury club than on candidates.
author: Ars Technica

title: Amazon uses homepage banner and app pop‑up to oppose NYC Delivery Protection Act
content:
Amazon has placed a vertical banner on its website and a pop‑up within its mobile app warning shoppers that the New York City Council could add up to $5 to each order. The banner, which appears when users are logged in, includes a button labeled “Act now.” A screenshot of the homepage banner was credited to Scharon Harding/Amazon.

According to Bloomberg, the message is intended to persuade shoppers not to support the proposed legislation. Amazon has not disclosed whether the notice is targeted to New York City residents based on account addresses, device location services, or another method. The company’s approach represents an unprecedented use of its consumer platform to address a specific municipal bill.
summary: Amazon is displaying a vertical banner on its website and a pop‑up in its app urging shoppers not to support a New York City bill. The banner warns that the NYC Council could add up to $5 per order and includes an “Act now” button, and Amazon has not explained how it targets users.
author: Ars Technica

title: Australian datacentre opposition gains momentum as Wingecaribee council backs moratorium
content:
A network of grassroots campaigners across Australia is sharing information to counter the rapid development of data‑centre projects. Their coordinated efforts aim to inform communities about the environmental and social impacts of new data‑centre infrastructure.

In March, Heather Champion tabled a council motion opposing a large gas plant intended to power a new data‑centre in the Southern Highlands of New South Wales. The motion did not pass.

Five months later, the local councillor for Wingecaribee introduced a new motion urging the federal government to impose a moratorium on new data‑centres. This motion was adopted unanimously by the council.
summary: A network of grassroots campaigners across Australia is sharing information to oppose the datacentre development boom. After Heather Champion's March council motion against a gas plant for a datacentre failed, a Wingecaribee councillor's motion calling for a federal moratorium on new datacentres passed unanimously five months later.

title: IMF head warns AI demand will push central banks to raise interest rates
content: Kristalina Georgieva says countries needed to be ready for tech rollout, adding: ‘You snooze, you lose’ Business live – latest updates Booming demand for artificial intelligence will force the world’s most powerful central banks to raise interest rates, the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has warned.
